subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
subtype: Approach: rescheduling with friends by phone [Action]
passage: Rain was drumming on the tin roof of the community centre when the scout leader read out the message: the mela ground was flooded, and Saturday's trip was off. Groans filled the room. Pema watched his friends' faces sag. "If we just go home," he thought, "nobody will plan it again, and it'll never happen." He borrowed his mother's phone from the waiting bench and, with the leader's nod, called Saurabh first. "Next Sunday? Same bus, ten o'clock?" Saurabh said yes. Then Tashi, then Ritika. The leader checked the notice board: the mela ran for two more weeks. By the time the parents arrived, "SUNDAY, 10, SAME BUS" was written on the whiteboard, and everyone was talking about the giant wheel again.

qa.q: Why was Saturday's trip off?
qa.a: The mela ground was flooded.

qa.q: What was Pema thinking as his friends' faces sagged?
qa.a: He was worried that without a new plan the trip would never happen, and felt determined to fix a date at once.

qa.q: What would you advise Pema if some friends can't make next Sunday?
qa.a: Offer two possible dates and choose the one most friends can manage, while everyone is still keen.

qa.q: How does the new plan feel to Saurabh?
qa.a: Saurabh says yes straight away, so his excitement seems to come right back.

grounding: After rain cancels a mela trip, a boy phones friends at once and settles a new date before the excitement fades.

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
subtype: Approach: rescheduling with friends by phone [Action]
passage: I'm Suraj, Madhav's neighbour. On Saturday morning we were all supposed to go to the Dussehra mela with my father. At eight it started pouring, and by nine my father said the mela ground would be mud. Madhav stood in our doorway, dripping, looking as if someone had cancelled his birthday. Then he pulled out his mother's old phone and started calling. First Kunal, then the twins. "Rain today, but the mela is on till next Sunday. Can your parents do next Sunday morning?" He wrote each answer on his hand. Then he came back to my father. "Uncle, everyone can do next Sunday. Can you?" My father laughed and said yes. I don't know how Madhav felt, but he was humming by lunch.

qa.q: What did Madhav write on his hand?
qa.a: Each friend's answer.

qa.q: What might Madhav have felt standing in the doorway?
qa.a: Very disappointed, as if someone had cancelled his birthday.

qa.q: What else could Madhav do in case next Sunday rains too?
qa.a: Agree a second back-up date with everyone now, so the plan doesn't fall apart again.

qa.q: How does Suraj see Madhav by lunch?
qa.a: Suraj notices Madhav humming, though Suraj cannot be sure how Madhav felt inside.

grounding: A neighbour watches a boy phone his friends right after the mela is rained off and fix a new day with everyone.

subtype: Approach: finishing homework first, then playing [Action]
passage: I'm Omkar, Nilesh's older brother, and we share a room and one game console. Until last month Nilesh played as soon as he got home, and at dinner he'd suddenly remember his maths and panic. He played with one eye on the clock, grumbling. Then he stuck a note on the console: HOMEWORK FIRST. Now he comes home, eats, does his homework at the desk, shows Mummy, and only then switches on. I noticed something. He laughs more when he plays now. He doesn't keep glancing at his school bag. Last night he beat my high score and went to sleep without the usual "Oh no, my worksheet!" I don't know exactly what changed inside him, but he seems lighter.

qa.q: What did the note on the console say?
qa.a: HOMEWORK FIRST.

qa.q: What does Nilesh laughing more while playing suggest?
qa.a: He feels relaxed and free of worry, so he enjoys the game more.

qa.q: What else could help Nilesh on days with a lot of homework?
qa.a: Splitting the homework into two parts with a short break, so the game still waits until it is done.

qa.q: How does Omkar see the change?
qa.a: Omkar sees Nilesh as lighter and happier, though not sure what changed inside.

grounding: An older brother notices that since a boy began finishing homework before gaming, he enjoys the game more without worry.

subtype: Approach: finishing homework first, then playing [Action]
passage:
Monday: Saurabh played his racing game from four to six, then did homework till ten, yawning, with his sister Sonali telling him to hurry. Even during the races he kept thinking about the science worksheet.
Wednesday: He wrote a sticky note and put it on the tablet cover: "Homework, then game." After school he did the worksheet and the maths at the kitchen table. At six he opened the game.
Friday: Sonali found him at five already packing his school bag, then flopping on the bed with the tablet. "You're playing early?" "Homework's done," he said. "Now I can actually enjoy it." He won three races and didn't glance at his bag once.

qa.q: What did Saurabh write on the sticky note?
qa.a: "Homework, then game."

qa.q: How did Saurabh feel while playing on Monday?
qa.a: Distracted and worried, because the science worksheet was still waiting.

qa.q: What else could help Saurabh keep the rule?
qa.a: Keeping the tablet out of reach until his bag is packed, so the order stays easy to follow.

qa.q: How does Sonali see the change?
qa.a: Sonali is surprised he's playing early, and sees him relaxed instead of rushing late at night.

grounding: Over a week, a boy switches to finishing homework before gaming and finds the game more fun without worry.

subtype: Approach: time-boxing game sessions [Action]
passage: Every weekday at five in their Chandigarh flat, Uma set the kitchen timer to forty minutes, put it next to the tablet and started her farm game. The first week was hard. When it rang, she'd groan, "One more harvest!" But she had made the rule herself after an argument with her mother, and she wanted to show she could keep it. So she saved and closed the game. By the third week she had started planning her forty minutes: harvest first, then build, then trade. When her cousin Amandeep visited and said, "Your mother lets you play only forty?", Uma said, "No. I let me play forty." Her mother, overhearing from the kitchen, smiled into the dal.

qa.q: How long does Uma play on weekdays?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Uma stop when the timer rang, even when it was hard?
qa.a: She felt determined to prove she could keep her own rule, and proud of it being hers.

qa.q: What else could Uma do on days she wants more time?
qa.a: Save the extra wish for the weekend or agree a special day with her mother, instead of stretching the weekday timer.

qa.q: How might Uma's mother feel overhearing her?
qa.a: Pleased and proud, which is why she smiles into the dal. 😊

grounding: A girl sets a forty-minute timer for weekday gaming and stops when it rings, making the limit her own rule.

subtype: Approach: time-boxing game sessions [Action]
passage:
"Beep-beep-beep!"
"Lakshmi, don't stop now, we're about to win!"
"Sorry, Sonali. Timer's done."
"Your mother isn't even home. Nobody's watching."
"I know. It's my timer, not hers."
"Your timer?"
"Forty minutes on school days. I set it. If I don't, I play till dinner and end up doing homework at ten, crying."
"But we're one level from the boss!"
"Then we beat him tomorrow at four-thirty." Lakshmi saved the game. "Want to make lemon water?"
"You're weird." Sonali sighed. "Fine. But tomorrow I'm bringing snacks and we start on the dot."
"Deal. And I'll set the timer."

qa.q: When will they play tomorrow?
qa.a: At four-thirty.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel stopping even though nobody was watching?
qa.a: Calm and firm, a little sorry to stop but proud that the rule is her own.

qa.q: What else could Lakshmi do if a level truly needs a few more minutes?
qa.a: Save it for the next day's forty minutes, as she did, rather than stretching today's limit.

qa.q: How does Sonali react?
qa.a: Sonali is annoyed at first, calling Lakshmi weird, then agrees to start on time tomorrow.

grounding: A girl stops gaming when her own forty-minute timer rings, even with no adult watching, because the limit is her rule.

subtype: Approach: just one more level [Pitfall]
passage:
"Nasir, dinner!"
"Coming, Ammi! One more round."
Later.
"Nasir, it's nine o'clock."
"Last one, I promise. I'm so close."
"What about your maths?"
"After this."
Later still.
"Nasir. It is ten o'clock."
"What? No. It was just eight-thirty." He looked at the clock and his stomach dropped. "Ammi, my maths! Twelve sums!"
"How many rounds did you play?"
"I don't know. One more, then one more..."
"And the sums?"
"Zero." He rubbed his eyes. "Can I do them in the morning?"
"You have school at seven-thirty. Sit. I'll make you tea, but you're doing them now."

qa.q: How many sums did Nasir have?
qa.a: Twelve sums.

qa.q: How did Nasir feel when he saw it was ten o'clock?
qa.a: Shocked and panicky; his stomach dropped.

qa.q: What else could Nasir try next time?
qa.a: Decide a stopping point before starting, like a timer or a set number of rounds, and do the maths first.

qa.q: How does Ammi respond at ten o'clock?
qa.a: Firm but kind: she makes him tea, but insists he does the sums now.

grounding: A boy keeps playing 'one more round' until it is ten at night with his maths still undone.

subtype: Approach: just one more level [Pitfall]
passage: Last winter I learned what "just one more round" really means. I'm Tenzin. I started a building game at seven, after dinner, telling myself I'd stop at eight and do my maths. At eight I said, one more round. At eight-thirty, one more. At some point my little sister Jaya came in and said, "Bhaiya, Mummy's asking about your homework," and I said, "Two minutes." Then I looked up and the clock said ten. Ten! My maths book was still in my bag with twenty sums. I did them half asleep and got seven wrong the next day. The game had no ending, so I never reached a place to stop. Now I decide my stopping point before I start.

qa.q: How many sums were waiting in the maths book?
qa.a: Twenty sums.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel on seeing the clock say ten?
qa.a: Shocked and panicked that two extra hours had vanished.

qa.q: What would you advise Tenzin to add to the new habit?
qa.a: A timer set before starting, so the chosen stopping point is announced, not just remembered.

qa.q: How might Jaya have seen the evening?
qa.a: Jaya passed on Mummy's question and got 'two minutes' back, so she may have felt ignored or worried.

grounding: Looking back, a boy describes playing 'one more round' until ten at night with maths undone, because the game had no stopping point.

subtype: Approach: weighing what matters more this week [Thinking]
passage:
"Siddharth, the new update's out! Coming online tonight?"
"Not this week, Hemant."
"What? It's the new map!"
"Science test on Friday. Chapters four and five."
"That's four days away."
"Four days to learn two chapters. The map will still be there on Saturday. The test won't wait."
"You're making it sound so serious."
"Look." Siddharth held up his notebook. He'd drawn two boxes: MUST DO NOW and CAN WAIT. "Test goes in 'must'. Game goes in 'can wait'. Saturday, I'm all yours."
"And if you finish early?"
"Then maybe Thursday night, one match. Maybe."
"Fine. But on Saturday you're carrying the team."

qa.q: What two boxes did Siddharth draw?
qa.a: MUST DO NOW and CAN WAIT.

qa.q: How does Siddharth seem to feel about skipping the new map?
qa.a: A little tempted, but calm and sure of his choice.

qa.q: What else could help Siddharth use the four days well?
qa.a: Splitting the two chapters across the days, so Thursday stays free for revision.

qa.q: How does Hemant react?
qa.a: Hemant is disappointed and teases him, then accepts Saturday.

grounding: Knowing a test is on Friday, a boy sorts what is urgent from what can wait and puts gaming off until the weekend.

subtype: Approach: weighing what matters more this week [Thinking]
passage: Last month I had a history test on Friday, and an online game tournament was starting on Wednesday. I'm Chaitanya. My cousin Uma was on the same team. On Monday I sat on my bed and asked myself two questions. What happens if I miss the tournament? We lose one week, and it runs again next month. What happens if I don't study? A bad mark that stays on my report card. So I told Uma to find a substitute until the weekend. It felt terrible for about an hour. Then I made a timetable: two lessons a day until Thursday. On Friday the test went fine. On Saturday I rejoined the team, and nobody even remembered I'd been gone.

qa.q: When did the online tournament start?
qa.a: On Wednesday.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya feel after telling Uma to find a substitute?
qa.a: Terrible for about an hour, then settled once the timetable was made.

qa.q: What else could Chaitanya have done during the test week?
qa.a: Played one short match after finishing the day's lessons, if the timetable allowed, instead of stopping completely.

qa.q: What was the week like for Uma?
qa.a: Uma had to find a substitute, which may have been a nuisance, but got the teammate back on Saturday.

grounding: Looking back, a child weighs a test against a game tournament and decides studying is urgent while the game can wait.

subtype: Approach: negotiating a fair deal with parents [Action]
passage:
Friday
Tonight was the big meeting. I made a proper proposal on a page: 1) Weekdays: no games, just my study plan from 5 to 7. 2) Saturday and Sunday: one hour of gaming each day. 3) If I miss the study plan on any day, I lose that weekend's hour. I showed it to Amma and Appa after dinner. Appa asked, "What about test weeks?" I added: 4) In test weeks, weekend gaming is half. Amma looked at Appa and said, "Let's try it for one month." ONE MONTH! I wrote it on the calendar in green. Wasim from my class says his parents would never agree to anything. I think it's because he never asks properly.
Lavanya

qa.q: What happens if Lavanya misses the study plan?
qa.a: Lavanya loses that weekend's hour of gaming.

qa.q: How does Lavanya feel after the meeting?
qa.a: Lavanya feels excited and proud, writing ONE MONTH on the calendar in green.

qa.q: What else could Lavanya do to keep the deal working?
qa.a: Lavanya could check the calendar with Amma and Appa each week, so small slips are talked about early.

qa.q: How might Amma and Appa see the proposal?
qa.a: They took it seriously, added a rule for test weeks and agreed to a month's trial.

grounding: A diary entry shows a child proposing weekend gaming in exchange for keeping a weekday study plan, and the parents agreeing to try it.

subtype: Approach: negotiating a fair deal with parents [Action]
passage: In their small town near Madurai, Keerthana's only gaming was on Appa's old phone, and every evening ended in an argument about it. On Sunday she sat with Amma and Appa on the thinnai and read out a plan she had written in her notebook. "On school days I study from six to eight and don't ask for the phone at all. On Saturday and Sunday I get one hour each. If I break the weekday rule even once, no phone that weekend." Appa scratched his chin. "And when your friend Shreya comes to play?" "Then we share the hour." Amma laughed. "One month, then. If the marks stay, it stays." Keerthana ran to write "Month 1" on the calendar.

qa.q: Where did Keerthana sit with her parents?
qa.a: On the thinnai.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel when Amma agreed to a month?
qa.a: Happy and excited, running to write 'Month 1' on the calendar.

qa.q: What else could Keerthana add to the plan?
qa.a: A short weekly check with her parents, so they can see the study hours are really happening.

qa.q: How might Appa see the plan?
qa.a: Appa is thoughtful, checking details like Shreya's visits, but open to trying it.

grounding: A girl offers her parents weekend gaming time in exchange for a weekday study plan, and they agree to a month's trial.

subtype: Approach: hiding the game and lying about homework [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday: "Homework done?" his mother, Sangeeta, asked. "Done," said Vishal, and went to his room, where he played his phone game under the blanket until nine.
Wednesday: He said it again. It wasn't. Two English worksheets and a maths page were stuffed, unfinished, at the bottom of his bag.
Friday: Sangeeta's phone buzzed during dinner. It was his class teacher: three assignments missing this week. She read the message twice and put the phone face down. She didn't shout. She just said, "You told me it was done. Twice." That weekend Vishal did all three assignments at the dining table, and the phone stayed with his mother. On Monday, when he said "Done", she opened his bag to check.

qa.q: What did the teacher's message say?
qa.a: Three assignments were missing this week.

qa.q: How might Vishal have felt when his mother said 'Twice'?
qa.a: Ashamed and guilty, caught in his own lie.

qa.q: What else could Vishal have done on Monday?
qa.a: Told the truth and asked for help with the worksheets, before the missing work piled up.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta respond?
qa.a: Quietly hurt; she doesn't shout, but she no longer takes his word and checks his bag.

grounding: Over a week, a boy lies about homework to play secretly, and the teacher's report brings both a marks problem and lost trust.

subtype: Approach: hiding the game and lying about homework [Pitfall]
passage: Pranav, you're hiding that phone under your pillow? Let me tell you what happened to me. When I was eleven, I, Lalit, had a small handheld game my uncle had brought back from abroad. Every evening I told my mother, "Homework finished," and played under the blanket with the sound off. For two weeks it worked. Then my class teacher sent a letter home: eight pieces of homework missing, marks cut, and would my parents please come to meet her. My mother read the letter at the kitchen table and didn't look at me for a long time. The marks I earned back, slowly. What took longer was her trust. For months she checked my notebook every night, and I knew I had earned that too.

qa.q: How many pieces of homework were missing?
qa.a: Eight.

qa.q: How did young Lalit feel when his mother didn't look up for a long time?
qa.a: Ashamed, knowing the lie had hurt her.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story caused the most trouble?
qa.a: Saying 'Homework finished' when it wasn't; doing the homework before playing would have avoided both the marks and the lost trust.

qa.q: How might Lalit's mother have felt reading the letter?
qa.a: Hurt and disappointed, betrayed by the evenings of 'Homework finished'.

grounding: An elder recalls lying about homework to play in secret, and how the teacher's letter cost both marks and a parent's trust.

subtype: Approach: using the game as a reward for goals [Thinking]
passage: The house was full of cousins for the weekend, and Madhuri still had two chapters of geography to finish before Monday. Her cousin Divyansh was already playing the racing game in the next room, and every cheer made her look up. "This isn't working," she thought. "If I sit here wishing I was playing, I'll never finish." Then an idea came. "The game is the prize. Two chapters, thirty minutes of racing. Not before." She told Divyansh, "Save me a car for eleven-thirty." She put in her earplugs, finished chapter one by ten-fifteen and chapter two by eleven twenty-five. At eleven-thirty she slid onto the floor beside him, grinning, with nothing left waiting at the back of her mind.

qa.q: When did Madhuri finish chapter two?
qa.a: At eleven twenty-five.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling when she thought 'This isn't working'?
qa.a: Frustrated and distracted, realising that wishing to play was stopping her from studying.

qa.q: What else could Madhuri try if the cheering still distracts her?
qa.a: Study in a quieter room for the two chapters, keeping the game as the reward afterwards.

qa.q: How might Divyansh experience the plan?
qa.a: Divyansh saves her a car and gets a relaxed cousin to race with at eleven-thirty.

grounding: In a noisy, busy house, a girl turns her game into a reward earned after two chapters, so it motivates rather than competes.

subtype: Approach: using the game as a reward for goals [Thinking]
passage: On weekday evenings in their Amritsar flat, Jasleen's puzzle game kept calling to her from the tablet on the shelf. Her friend Zainab played it straight after school, but Jasleen had noticed something: whenever she played first, she studied badly afterwards and felt guilty. So she made a new deal with herself and wrote it on a sticky note on the tablet: "2 chapters = 30 minutes." On Tuesday she did chapters six and seven of science, testing herself with the questions at the end. Then she set a timer and played, and the thirty minutes felt like a real prize. By Friday she had done eight chapters and played four evenings, and her mother hadn't said "Put that down" once.

qa.q: What does the sticky note say?
qa.a: "2 chapters = 30 minutes."

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel when she played before studying?
qa.a: Guilty, and she studied badly afterwards.

qa.q: What else could help Jasleen on days with harder chapters?
qa.a: She could make the reward one chapter plus a short game on those days, so the deal still feels fair.

qa.q: What has changed for Jasleen's mother?
qa.a: Her mother hasn't had to say 'Put that down' once, which is probably a relief.

grounding: A girl makes her game a reward for finishing two chapters, turning it into a motivator rather than a competitor for time.

subtype: Approach: noticing tiredness and changing the routine [Revision]
passage: Shankar woke with a jolt to laughter. His cheek was on his maths notebook, and Varun, beside him, was whispering, "Sir's looking at you." The teacher only said, "Late night?", but Shankar's face burned for the rest of the day. He had played his football game till past midnight again. On the bus home he thought about it. "Four nights this week. Four mornings like a zombie." That evening he talked to his father. "Can I play from four-thirty to five-thirty, before tuition, instead of at night?" His father agreed, and Shankar himself suggested the console go on top of the fridge at nine. By the next week he was wide awake in maths, and Varun had to find something else to laugh at.

qa.q: What did the teacher say?
qa.a: "Late night?"

qa.q: How did Shankar feel after waking up in class?
qa.a: Embarrassed; his face burned for the rest of the day.

qa.q: What else could help Shankar keep the new routine?
qa.a: Keeping the console out of his room at night altogether, so the nine o'clock rule is easy to follow.

qa.q: How might Varun see the change?
qa.a: Varun now has an alert friend beside him in maths instead of a sleepy one to laugh at.

grounding: After falling asleep in class from late gaming, a boy moves his playtime to the afternoon and puts the console away by nine.

subtype: Approach: noticing tiredness and changing the routine [Revision]
passage:
"Pankaj-bhaiya, I fell asleep in science today."
"In class?"
"On the desk. Ma'am woke me up by tapping the duster. Everyone laughed."
"Because you played till one again."
"Twelve-thirty." Lokesh sighed. "I keep saying one more match. I'm tired every morning."
"So what will you do?"
"I was thinking on the way home. If I play after school, from five to six, I'm done before dinner. And the console..." He hesitated. "The console goes in your room at nine. You keep it."
"Me? You'll bang on my door."
"I won't. That's the point. If it's in my room, I'll play."
"Fine. From nine o'clock it's mine till morning."
"And if I ask for it back, don't give it."

qa.q: Until what time did Lokesh play last night?
qa.a: Twelve-thirty.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel when everyone laughed?
qa.a: Embarrassed, and fed up with being tired every morning.

qa.q: What else could help Lokesh stick to the plan?
qa.a: Setting an alarm at five to six, so the afternoon session ends without an argument with himself.

qa.q: How does Pankaj-bhaiya respond?
qa.a: He teases a little but agrees to hold the console every night.

grounding: After falling asleep in class from late gaming, a boy moves his playtime to the afternoon and hands over the console at nine.

subtype: Approach: playing a game with friends instead of alone [Thinking]
passage: In the common room of the girls' hostel, the old game console was free most evenings, and Zainab had started slipping down alone after dinner. One level turned into ten. On Wednesday she looked at the clock and realised she had played for two hours by herself and still hadn't written her letter home. Sitting on the stairs, she thought about it. "When I play alone, there's nobody to say stop. When my cousins play, we laugh more, and it ends when the warden calls lights-out." Her cousins, Amandeep and Rubina, lived a floor above. So she made a rule: games only on evenings they came down. That first Saturday the three of them played until the warden's bell, shouting at the screen, and it felt like twice the fun in half the time.

qa.q: How long had Zainab played alone on Wednesday?
qa.a: Two hours by herself.

qa.q: What was Zainab thinking on the stairs?
qa.a: Uneasy about the lost time, she realised that playing alone had no natural stopping point.

qa.q: What else could Zainab do on evenings her cousins are busy?
qa.a: Write her letters or read, keeping the console for the shared evenings.

qa.q: How might Amandeep and Rubina experience the new rule?
qa.a: They get a cousin to play with and livelier evenings together.

grounding: A hostel girl who feels the pull of playing alone decides to game only with her cousins, which limits time and adds fun.

subtype: Approach: playing a game with friends instead of alone [Thinking]
passage: I'm Preeti, Devika's older cousin, and I live in the same building. Last term, whenever I came up, Devika was alone in her room with the tablet and earphones, hardly looking up while her mother called her name. Then one day Devika told me, "I'm only going to play when you and Rinku are here." I thought she was joking. But now, when Rinku and I come up on Sunday afternoons, she pulls out the tablet and we play the island game together, all three crowded on the bed, arguing about which bridge to build. When we leave, she puts the tablet back on the shelf. On weekdays I see her reading on the balcony instead. I don't know what made her decide, but she seems happier.

qa.q: When do Preeti and Rinku come up?
qa.a: On Sunday afternoons.

qa.q: Why might Devika have decided to play only with her cousins?
qa.a: Playing alone may have felt lonely and hard to stop, while playing together is more fun and ends naturally.

qa.q: What else could Devika do if her cousins stop visiting for a while?
qa.a: Agree a short weekend time with her mother, so the game stays limited without them.

qa.q: How does Preeti see the change?
qa.a: Preeti thinks Devika seems happier, though Preeti isn't sure what made Devika decide.

grounding: A cousin notices a girl now plays only when her cousins visit, which limits her gaming and makes it more fun.
